### Reading notes: Second quantisation impressions [@secondQuantisationBook2010]:

Second quantisation seems to be general framework of ladder operators and associated commutation relations; which is a familiar concept. Apparently generalises nicely to N-body quantum physics.

Chapter motivates second quantisation by highlighting computational issues w/many body QM due to indistinguishablity, symmetrization.antisymmetrization, and the exchange of particle numbers.

#### Second quantisation basics
It then covers the "apparatus of second quantization".

Compares representation of labelling particles in state individually to simply counting the number of particles in each state (I.E $\ket{1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3}$ becomes $\ket{4, 2, 1}$). This is the "occuptation number representation". Also note the "Fock space" $\mathcal{F}$; made up of basis states $\{ \ket{n_{i}} \}$ w/out occupation num condition $\sum n_i = N$. Therefore many body state can be represented as $\ket{\Psi}=\sum_{n_{i}} c_{n_i}\ket{n_{i}}$.

Within this framework, ladder operators can be constructed to act on $\mathcal{F}$:

$a_{i}^{\dagger}\ket{n_{1},...,n_{i},...}=(n_{i}+1)^{1/2}\zeta^{s_{i}}\ket{n_{1},...n_{i}+1,...}$
$s_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}n_{j}$

Note that in the fermionic case, the $n_{i}+1$ operation is a mod 2 operation $n_{i}+1 \equiv (n_{i}+1)\%2$
Utility of this; can generate all states by repeated application of $a_{i}^{\dagger}$ to vacuum state:

$\ket{n_{1},...}=\prod_{i}\frac{1}{(n_{i}!)^{1/2}}(a_{i}^{\dagger})^{n_{i}\ket{0}}$

::: {.column-margin}
Wierd notation used by chapter for commutation/anti-commutation relations:

$[A,B]_{\zeta}=AB-\zeta AB$

$[A,B]_{\zeta=+1}=[A,B]_{+}=AB-AB$ // commutator

$[A,B]_{\zeta=-1}=[A,B]_{-}=AB+AB=\{A,B\}$ // anticomutator
:::

Note that:

$[a_i,a_j^{\dagger}]_{\zeta}=\delta_{ij}$

$[a_i,a_j]_{\zeta}=0$

$[a_i^{\dagger},a_j^{\dagger}]_{\zeta}=0$

#### practical aspects:
The chapter continues into the "practical aspects" of this framework.

::: {.callout-note title="Single particle base transforms"}
Firstly; switching between single particle bases $\{ \lambda \} \to \{ \widetilde{\lambda} \}$ - the operators transform as:

$a_{\widetilde{\lambda}}^{\dagger} = \sum_{\lambda}\braket{\lambda|\widetilde{\lambda}}a_{\lambda}^{\dagger}$

$a_{\widetilde{\lambda}} = \sum_{\lambda}\braket{\widetilde{\lambda}|\lambda}a_{\lambda}$

where $\lambda$ represents a particular particle state in a particular single particle basis.
For continuous quantum numbers (I.E, pos) the sum becomes integrals as:

$a_{\lambda}=\int_{0}^{L}dx\braket{\lambda|x}a(x)$

$a(x)=\sum_{k}\braket{x|\lambda}a_{\lambda}$
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Single particle operators"}
Secondly operators acting on single particles w/single party operator $o_{n}$ on nth particle typically become $\mathcal{O_{1}}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}o_{n}$.

Typical example noted is momentum:
$T=\sum_{n}\frac{p_{n}^2}{2m}$

Also introduces "occupation number operator" which counts #particles in state:

$n_{\lambda}=a_{\lambda}^{\dagger}a_{\lambda}$

Which is useful for actually constructing $\mathcal{O_{1}}$. Given $o=\sum_{i}o_{\lambda_i}\ket{\lambda_i}\bra{\lambda_i}$, $o_{\lambda_i}=\braket{\lambda_i | o | \lambda_i}$. Skipping over details i'm uninterested in rn, the general result is:

$\mathcal{O_1}=\sum_{\mu\nu}\braket{\mu |o|\nu}a_{\lambda}^{\dagger}a_{\lambda}$
:::

The chapter then goes into concrete examples to cement these ideas - not immediately relevant, but earmarking p48 in case useful for later.

### Examining provided code:
First code block is just some library setup.

Second code block sets up spectral function (currently set to a semi-circle) as function of $\omega$. It then initialises an empty 2D hamiltonian array for the bath sites. Unsure why 2D; my understanding is that a 1D list would encapsulate the bath perfectly fine. Potentially initialising all timesteps and fills them throughout the sim? Oooooh, nvm, its the hamiltonian matrix.
Plots the spectral function over $\omega$.

::: {.column-margin}
Sidenote; just realized Julia indicates vector maths using a "." notation (I.E, scalar addition ```a+b``` becomes vector addition ```a.+b```)
:::

Third code block sets up initial state using Fermi Dirac stats: 

$\mathcal{f}(\beta, \mu, E) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{\beta E-\beta\mu}}$

The simulation assumes no initial correlations; therefore initial correlation matrix is diagonalised and filled with $\mathcal{f}(\beta, \mu, E)$ for all corresponding system and bath sites:

$C_{ii} = \mathcal{f}(\beta, \mu, E_i)$

Third code block sets up this initial correlation matrix.

Fourth/fifth code blocks illustrate fact that $C_{t=0}$ is diagnolized in site, not hamiltonian basis.

Sixth/seventh code block builds unitary time evolution:

$U(t) = e^{-iHt}$

And build function to evolve correlation matrix over time t.
::: {.column-margin}
Sidenote; another julia syntax note; matrix complex conjugate is indicated as ```H'```
:::

Code block 9 (and surrounding commented out code blocks) compute the correlation matrix over a range of times. The commented out bits inc a computationally slower algorithm (the main method is iterative), and a commented out plot.

Code blocks 10, 11 compute and plot the reduced density matrix element corresponding to the occupation of the system. Recalling [@ProjectOutline2026], the reduced density matrix follows:

$\rho_S(t)=(\begin{array}{cc}
1-\mathbf{C}_{11}(t) & 0 \\
0 & \mathbf{C}_{11}(t)
\end{array})$

where the first element corresponds to the system.

Code block 12 computes the occupation for the bath at the end of the sim.

Final section asks the following questions:

#### On convergence

#### On the physics

* What happens to the covariance matrix as we time evolve? Does it show any emergent structure? 
* How do these structures relate to the initial choice of the spectral function?
* Let's perturb the spectral function: can we see long-lived memory effects building up?

Which seem to be starting points for my investigations.

[@juliaPerformanceTips] is an article detailing how to get most out of Julia so will have a quick look through there.

#### julia performance tips reading [@juliaPerformanceTips]

* performance critical code should be inside functions
* avoid unsigned global variables

Tried [@stackoverflowJuliaVsPython2022] moving everything into a function in case that worked; it didnt. However i suspect that the code requires broader optimisation. The fact that the basic adding arrays test favours python so strongly is incredibly odd... Apparently global variables are REALLY bad in julia, so maybe its that?

Have just measured the one case where there is a global variable and thats the issue.
THis block of code:
```
    Udt = unitary(dt)
    UdtT = Udt'
    Css = Dict(0.0 => C0)
    key = 0.0
    for t in times[2:end]
        #println(key, " ",t)
        Css[t] = Udt * Css[key] * UdtT
        key = t
    end
```
is whats causing issues. If the global variable key is to blame, editing the code to not use it may help? it may also be an issue of the matrix multiplcation occuring in that loop. Also dictionary access?
As i see it 3 potential issues:

* Matrix multiplications are computationally awful
* the "key" variable is to my knowledge global, and is getting reassigned every iteration - apparently Julia dislikes this
* assigning the data to a dictionary which intuition would suggest is a less efficient data structure

Have reworked it so that instead of assigning key, doing it by iteration - seems to shave 5-10sec. Will examine the dictionary storage next because that also seems to be causing issues. Switching to array doesn't seem to have saved time. Seemingly matrix multiplication is main cause of issues...
